text: A Java application logs a specially crafted string containing a JNDI lookup submitted via an HTTP request header. The LDAP-referenced malicious class is fetched and executed on the server, giving the attacker unauthenticated remote code execution.

An attacker sends crafted SMBv1 packets to a Windows file-sharing service, exploiting a buffer overflow to gain remote code execution and worm to other machines on the network, which are then encrypted for ransom.

An unauthenticated attacker sends specially crafted requests to a Windows Remote Desktop Protocol service, triggering a use-after-free vulnerability to achieve remote code execution with no user interaction required.

An attacker already on the internal network exploits a cryptographic flaw in the Netlogon Remote Protocol to reset the domain controller's computer account password and impersonate it, gaining full domain administrator privileges.
A low-privileged local user abuses the Windows Print Spooler service to load an arbitrary DLL with SYSTEM privileges, escalating from a standard account to full administrative control of the host.
An attacker sends an HTTP request with a malicious environment variable value to a CGI script, exploiting a Bash parsing flaw to execute arbitrary shell commands on the web server.
An attacker submits a crafted Content-Type header to a Struts2-based web application, triggering an OGNL injection that executes arbitrary operating system commands on the underlying server.

An unauthenticated attacker sends a crafted HTTP request to an on-premises Microsoft Exchange server, exploiting a server-side request forgery flaw to authenticate as the Exchange server itself and access mailbox data.
Attackers exploited a SQL injection vulnerability in a public-facing managed file transfer web application to gain unauthorized database access and plant web shells used for mass data exfiltration.

A victim opens a malicious Word document; when the document is previewed, it invokes the Microsoft Support Diagnostic Tool through a remote template to execute a PowerShell command without macros or clicking 'Enable Content'.

A phishing email attachment is a Word document embedding a malformed OLE object that exploits a memory corruption bug in the legacy Equation Editor component, executing attacker code as soon as the file is opened.

An attacker sends a specially crafted email containing an extended MAPI property with a UNC path. Outlook automatically connects to the attacker's SMB server upon receipt, leaking the victim's NTLM hash without any user interaction.
An unauthenticated attacker sends a crafted HTTP resource request to a Fortinet SSL VPN web portal, exploiting a path traversal flaw to read a session file and obtain plaintext VPN credentials.

An attacker forges a certificate for a trusted software publisher by exploiting a flaw in Windows' elliptic-curve cryptography validation, allowing malicious code to appear as though it were signed by a legitimate, trusted source.

An adversary with local administrator rights on a compromised host runs a tool to dump the memory of the LSASS process, extracting plaintext passwords, password hashes, and Kerberos tickets for cached user sessions.

source: Incident behavior: PowerShell in-memory second stage
text: The attacker executes a base64-encoded PowerShell command that downloads a second-stage payload from a remote server and runs it entirely in memory to avoid writing files to disk.

Employees received an email with a password-protected ZIP attachment containing a macro-enabled Excel spreadsheet. Opening it and enabling macros silently downloaded and installed a remote access trojan.
After the initial compromise, the attacker created a scheduled task configured to run a malicious script every time the machine started, ensuring their access survived reboots.
The implant beacons out to its command-and-control server roughly every 60 seconds over HTTPS on port 443, blending in with normal web traffic to receive tasking and exfiltrate data.

An attacker with a valid domain user account requests Kerberos service tickets for accounts with registered service principal names, then extracts the tickets to crack the service account passwords offline.

An unauthenticated attacker sends a crafted HTTP request containing directory traversal sequences to a Citrix Application Delivery Controller, allowing arbitrary file write and remote code execution on the appliance.

An unauthenticated attacker sends a crafted URL to a public-facing Confluence Server instance, triggering an OGNL expression injection that results in arbitrary command execution on the underlying server.
An unauthenticated attacker sends an oversized request to a Citrix NetScaler ADC/Gateway appliance, triggering a stack buffer overflow that grants remote code execution on the device.

Having previously compromised the krbtgt account's password hash, the attacker forges a Kerberos ticket-granting ticket offline, allowing them to impersonate any domain user and access any resource in the domain indefinitely.
The attacker captures an NTLM password hash from a compromised workstation and uses it directly to authenticate to other systems on the network without ever cracking the hash into plaintext.
The attacker extracts a Kerberos ticket from a compromised machine's memory and replays it on a different host to authenticate as the ticket's original owner without knowing their password.

The attacker places a malicious DLL with the same filename as a library expected by a legitimate, signed application in that application's directory, so the trusted program loads and executes the attacker's code when it runs.
After compromising a Linux server, the attacker adds an entry to the crontab that re-downloads and executes their backdoor every hour, ensuring their access survives process termination or reboot.

The attacker authenticates to the organization's SSL VPN gateway using employee credentials purchased from a criminal marketplace, gaining an initial foothold on the internal network with no exploit or malware required.

source: Incident behavior: cloud role assumption abuse
text: After compromising a low-privileged cloud service account, the attacker discovers it is permitted to assume a highly privileged IAM role and uses that misconfiguration to obtain administrative control of the cloud environment.

The malware encodes stolen files into a series of subdomain labels and sends them as DNS queries to an attacker-controlled name server, exfiltrating the data outside of its normal command-and-control channel.

source: Incident behavior: ransomware disabling shadow copies
text: Before encrypting files, the ransomware runs vssadmin to delete all Volume Shadow Copies on the system, preventing the victim from restoring their files from local backups.

source: Incident behavior: clearing Windows event logs
text: After completing their objectives, the attacker runs wevtutil to clear the Security and System event logs on the compromised host in an attempt to remove evidence of their activity.
The attacker abuses the built-in certutil.exe utility, passing it a URL flag to download a second-stage payload from an external server, avoiding the need to bring their own download tool.
Using a compromised low-privileged domain account, the attacker queries Active Directory to list every computer object joined to the domain in order to plan lateral movement.

source: Incident behavior: business email compromise inbox rule
text: After phishing an executive's credentials, the attacker logs into the mailbox and creates a hidden rule that silently forwards all incoming invoices to an external address the attacker controls.

Before sending stolen documents out of the network, the attacker compresses them into a single password-protected ZIP archive using a built-in command-line utility to reduce their size and obscure their contents.

Malware running on the victim's browser extracts an active authenticated session cookie for a corporate web application and sends it to the attacker, who imports it into their own browser to access the account without needing a password.
Using compromised local administrator credentials, the attacker uses PsExec to remotely install and start a Windows service on another host, causing it to execute their payload.

From a freshly compromised host, the attacker runs a scanning tool against the internal network range to identify which other hosts have SMB, RDP, and WinRM ports open before deciding where to move next.
